rationale: B wins because it has the discipline to keep three real stories and not pad the set with a half-proven trend piece. Its strongest line, "Bumble's AI relaunch is a turnaround bet with no numbers yet," is an actual markets story with the missing metric baked into the frame. A has strong material, especially "If AI Writes the First Message, Is Bumble's Women-First Model Still Feminist?," but then it wanders into "Users Push Back as Dating Apps Embrace AI Matchmaking" and starts making category claims the update did not earn.
gaps_in_A: "Bumble is the highest-profile dating platform to deploy AI matchmaking and AI-assisted message writing at scale" is invented altitude. The update gives one company relaunch, not category leadership or scale.
"The relaunch is the stated answer to the subscriber slide" overstates the record. The update says the relaunch follows declining paying users, not that Bumble positioned it as the answer.

"Users Push Back as Dating Apps Embrace AI Matchmaking" overlaps the contrarian AI-authenticity angle and needs other-app evidence the set admits it does not have. Keeping it is padding with a footnote.
"Is Bumble's Women-First Model Still Feminist?" is a sharper story than most, but "feminist" imports brand politics not stated in the update. It may be true historically; it is not supplied here.
gaps_in_B: "The app that made women message first will now help write the message" is powerful, but it slightly outruns the facts unless the AI specifically helps write the woman's first message. To its credit, the proof section catches this.
"funding-mechanics" is the wrong story type for a public-company turnaround angle. Call it markets, public-company, or investor-data; do not make reporters decode your taxonomy.

"the market is pricing it before any post-relaunch paying-user data exists" is plausible but still an inference. The update says the stock fell and post-relaunch users are unreported; it does not give current market reaction to the relaunch.
